slides.0.title: Level 3 final assessment
slides.0.subtitle: Viticulture, style, comparison, regulation and industry
slides.1.title: Level 3 review: viticulture and winemaking
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Hazards and climate
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Frost, mildew, heatwaves and hail; the direction of climate change is earlier harvests, higher potential alcohol and lower total acidity (specific figures are dated and sourced and are outside the assessment)
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Adaptation and new varieties
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Adjust harvest, canopy, fertiliser and whether to run MLF; Voltis: ≤ 5% of the vineyard and ≤ 10% of a blend, a new variety; certification and herbicide targets shift over time
slides.1.highlights.2.title: The style spectrum
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Reductive and oxidative form a spectrum; oak barrels allowed, wood chips banned; MLF is a choice; reserve wine sustains NV style; time on lees differs from time after disgorgement
slides.1.highlights.3.title: Dosage
slides.1.highlights.3.content: Brut Nature <3 (no added sugar), Extra Brut 0–6, Brut <12, Extra Dry 12–17, Sec 17–32, Demi-Sec 32–50, Doux >50 g/L; dosage balances acid and shapes style, not just sweetness
slides.1.content: Outside the assessment: specific climate figures, certification shares, trial details beyond the Voltis limits and individual producers’ practices.
slides.2.title: Level 3 review: comparison and regulation
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Soil contrast
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Central Champagne is Cretaceous chalk; Chablis and the Côte des Bar are Jurassic Kimmeridgian marl; Blanc de Blancs is white grapes only and Blanc de Noirs black grapes only
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Other sparkling wines
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Cava, Franciacorta, English and Crémant are bottle-fermented (traditional method) while Prosecco is typically tank-method; ageing months and areas are single-source comparison material and are not assessed
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Label codes
slides.2.highlights.2.content: NM house, RM grower-maker, CM cooperative, RC cooperative member selling under own name, SR growers’ society, ND distributor, MA buyer’s brand; the code does not imply quality
slides.2.highlights.3.title: Conditions for claims and name protection
slides.2.highlights.3.content: Millésime: 100% of grapes from that year (85% generally); single variety 100%; Prestige has no legal definition; within the EU “méthode champenoise” is reserved for Champagne
slides.2.content: Outside the assessment: other regions’ ageing numbers, Crémant minimum ageing, the year of the ban (1994) and Premier Cru 42/44.
slides.3.title: Level 3 review: industry and essays
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Market trend
slides.3.highlights.0.content: Shipments have fallen for three years; exports are over half; recent pressure leans towards French demand; revenue has fallen less than volume (specific figures are dated and not assessed)
slides.3.highlights.1.title: The three supply levers
slides.3.highlights.1.content: Marketable yield (set by the Comité each summer) → reserve (holds the surplus) → stock (finished wine). This is supply management, not a quality decision
slides.3.highlights.2.title: SAT and blind logic
slides.3.highlights.2.content: Method first (autolysis, mousse), then origin (acidity and ripeness), grape last; a conclusion needs reasons, using BLIC: balance, length, intensity, complexity
slides.3.highlights.3.title: The MW essay approach
slides.3.highlights.3.content: Define → arguments for and against with evidence → limits → a position; mark claims as claims; do not treat disputed numbers as settled; exam specifications follow the latest official WSET/IMW material
slides.3.content: Outside the assessment: exact shipment and revenue figures, years of stock, group shareholdings and deal details, market shares.
slides.4.componentProps.slide.title: 📋 Level 3 final assessment
Under the INAO specification, what are the minimum ageing periods from tirage before release for NV and Vintage?
A. 15 months / 36 months
B. 12 months / 24 months
C. 24 months / 48 months
D. 9 months / 18 months
NV 15 months, Vintage 36 months, counted from tirage (Level 2).
What does the specification say is the cap on vintage wine?
A. Up to 100%, reserve wine allowed
B. No more than 50%
C. No more than 80% of that year’s wine, with no reserve wine
D. No limit at all
This is the yearly quota; that 100% of grapes must come from the stated year is a separate rule (DGCCRF).
Which sub-region has no Grand Cru or Premier Cru villages?
A. Montagne de Reims
B. Côte des Bar (Aube)
C. Côte des Blancs
D. Vallée de la Marne
All 17 + 42 villages on the INAO list are in the Marne; none are in the Aube (Level 2).
What are the rules for Voltis?
A. One of the eight traditional varieties with no proportion limit
B. Allowed only for rosé
C. Banned in Champagne
D. A mildew-resistant new variety; up to 5% of the vineyard and 10% of any blend
Voltis is a new variety approved for trial at the end of 2022 (ch-l3-1 and Level 2).
What is the consistent direction of climate change in Champagne?
A. Later harvests, higher acidity
B. Earlier harvests, higher potential alcohol, lower acidity
C. Much more rain, lower sugar
D. No change
Specific figures vary by year and source but the direction is consistent (ch-l3-1).
In a warm, low-acid year, what is the main effect of skipping MLF?
A. It keeps malic acid and preserves acidity and tension
B. It raises alcohol
C. It makes the wine sweeter
D. It shortens the second fermentation
MLF converts malic to lactic acid; skipping it keeps acidity (ch-l3-2).
What does Brut Nature mean?
A. Residual sugar 12–17 g/L
B. Residual sugar 32–50 g/L
C. Residual sugar below 3 g/L with no added sugar
D. Residual sugar above 50 g/L
DGCCRF: Brut nature has no added sugar and residual sugar below 3 g/L.
Which statement about the soils of central Champagne and Chablis is correct?
A. Both are Cretaceous chalk
B. Both are volcanic soils
C. Central Champagne is Kimmeridgian and Chablis is chalk
D. Central Champagne is Cretaceous chalk; Chablis is Jurassic Kimmeridgian marl
Both are calcareous, but the geological age and rock type differ (Levels 1 and 3).
What does the label code “NM” stand for?
A. négociant-manipulant: buys grapes, must or wine and completes at least the final stages in-house; the large houses belong here
B. récoltant-manipulant: a grower making and selling its own wine
C. coopérative de manipulation: a cooperative
D. marque d’acheteur: a buyer’s brand
DGCCRF: NM is the house category; the code does not imply quality (Level 3).
Who sets the yearly marketable yield?
A. Each house individually
B. The Comité Champagne (each summer)
C. The European Commission
D. The French president
The Comité Champagne, made up of the SGV and UMC, sets it each summer (Levels 2 and 3).
What does the specification say about reserve wine?
A. Up to 12,400 kg/ha and it may carry a vintage
B. Reserve wine is banned
C. It must go 100% into vintage wine
D. Each producer has a reserve ceiling, and reserve wine cannot carry a vintage
This is the INAO rule (Level 2); sources differ on the exact ceiling (8,000 vs 10,000), so the figure is not tested.
What is the status of the term “méthode champenoise” in the EU?
A. Any sparkling wine may use it freely
B. Only Crémant may use it
C. Reserved for Champagne; other regions say traditional method (méthode traditionnelle) and similar
D. Only Prosecco may use it
The year of the ban is a single-source statement and is not assessed; just know that within the EU the term is reserved for Champagne (ch-l3-4).
